title: Generics — compile-time type safety, no explicit casts
shortTitle: What are generics and why do we need them?

s1_definition.profdef: Generics add compile-time type safety to collections and classes. Declaring `List<String>` lets the compiler reject any attempt to add the wrong type and removes the need for explicit casts when reading elements, turning a class of runtime `ClassCastException` bugs into compile errors that are caught before the code ever runs.
s1_definition.analogy: Without generics a filing drawer accepts anything — cheques, cash, even a lunch box — and you only discover the mistake when you reach in and crash. With generics the drawer is labelled "cheques only", and the compiler refuses the wrong item at filing time, long before anyone gets hurt.
s1_definition.oneliner: Generics give compile-time type safety and remove casts, converting runtime ClassCastException into compile errors.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Generics add compile-time type safety to collections and classes. Declaring `List<String>` lets the compiler reject any attempt to add the wrong type and removes the need for explicit casts when reading elements, turning a class of runtime `ClassCastException` bugs into compile errors that are caught before the code ever runs.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Without generics a filing drawer accepts anything — cheques, cash, even a lunch box — and you only discover the mistake when you reach in and crash. With generics the drawer is labelled "cheques only", and the compiler refuses the wrong item at filing time, long before anyone gets hurt.

**One line to remember:** Generics give compile-time type safety and remove casts, converting runtime ClassCastException into compile errors.

sections.s3_banking: At the National Bank of India this came up directly when handling generics and compile-time type safety. Rajesh holds savings account SAV2001 with a balance of 1,000,000 rupees and Priya holds current account CUR3001 with 250,000 rupees, and the team needed the collection behaviour to be exactly correct so balances and account lists were never wrong. The runnable demo below reproduces the situation and proves the behaviour with a small test.

The input is the pair of accounts SAV2001 (Rajesh) and CUR3001 (Priya) with BigDecimal balances.

Step 1: the service loads both accounts into the chosen collection.

Step 2: the topic-specific operation runs against the collection.

Step 3: the result is observed and the generic list rejected a wrong-typed value at compile time.

Step 4: the service returns the correct result to the caller and logs it.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Generics provide compile-time type safety and eliminate explicit casts. By parameterising a collection, for example as a list of String account identifiers, the compiler rejects the wrong type immediately and removes a whole category of runtime ClassCastException failures.

In the National Bank codebase I insisted on fully parameterised collections everywhere, so lists of account identifiers such as SAV2001 and CUR3001 and lists of BigDecimal amounts could never be mixed by accident. Because these errors were caught at compile time rather than in production, the money-handling paths were far safer, which is exactly what you want in a banking system.

In an interview I would stress that I always use BigDecimal for money, keep map keys immutable, and pick the collection whose ordering and complexity match the banking access pattern, because in a system that moves real money, choosing the wrong data structure is not a style issue, it is a correctness and reliability issue.

keyPoints: Generics: compile-time type safety without explicit casting
List<String> prevents adding Integer — caught at compile time
Without generics: List stores Object, requires casting, ClassCastException at runtime
Introduced in Java 5 — backward compatible via type erasure
